newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus isolated as Lukashenko wins gamble.
newsitem.headline: Belarus isolated as Lukashenko wins gamble.

text.p: Belarus, called an island of stability by its hardline president, was looking isolated, friendless and full of uncertainty on Monday after he gambled and won a controversial referendum on expanding his powers.

Even big brother Russia was less than effusive with its praise for little Belarus on its western border, where President Alexander Lukashenko was setting about realising his dream of extending his term beyond 2000.
In Moscow, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin called the result "normal" and said: "It's a matter for Belarus."
The Kremlin press service said Chernomyrdin and President Boris Yeltsin had discussed the poll and stressed Russia's "timely" efforts had "prevented a social explosion".
"Flabbergasted, I think, is my response to that," one political analyst who asked not to be identified said, pouring scorn on the notion that Russia's intervention had helped.
Chernomyrdin would have every right to be irritated with the neighbouring former Soviet republic of 10 million.

He sat up all night with its main political rivals -- Lukashenko and parliament leader Semyon Sharetsky -- to mediate a peace deal signed at dawn on Friday but it collapsed in ruins almost as soon as the ink dried.
The Russian leadership was not openly critical, but ORT television, which tends to follow the wind from the Kremlin, on Monday blamed Lukashenko for the breakdown of the agreement.

Analysts said Russia could not stay indifferent to domestic events in Belarus, its partner in a much-vaunted two-state community. But influencing the stubborn and wily Lukashenko was no simple matter even for the Kremlin, "unless someone has a magic card or a silver bullet", as one put it.
Belarus is dependent on Russia for gas and oil supplies and has so alienated international lending bodies that they have frozen loans to the republic between Russia and Poland.

Critics of Lukashenko's referendum, in which he won a mandate to rewrite the constitution -- but only by ignoring the old one -- say it gives him carte blanche to crush resistance to his authoritarian rule in all institutions.

The new constitution is "dangerous for human rights" and "does not respect the principle of separation of powers" by depriving parliament of a chance to work as a counterweight, a Council of Europe analysis said earlier this month.
Perhaps aware that Moscow was less than delighted with events, Lukashenko turned a genial face to Europe on Monday.
To the disbelief of Western analysts, he declared he wanted to join the European Union. "Belarus is a European state and it must be in the family of European states," he said.
Hours later Britain delivered a letter from the Irish EU presidency expressing "deep concern" at the situation.
Belarus is the only European country outside former Yugoslavia not to have joined the Council of Europe and on current form is moving even further away from its minimum human rights standards.
On Sunday more than 80 percent of its electorate agreed with Lukashenko the death penalty should be kept in force.

Other former Soviet republics including Russia have agreed to phase out the death penalty as part of the price of admission to the Council of Europe, set up after World War Two to promote human rights and democracy.
Another sign of Belarus's isolation came when Lukashenko said a ceremony to mark the withdrawal of the last former Soviet missiles from Belarus would not take place on Tuesday.
"We want the defence ministers of Russia, Belarus and the United States to be there," he said, adding that the Americans had "some problems" and the ceremony would not happen.
The U.S. embassy is by far Lukashenko's most outspoken Western critic in Minsk and Washington has no plans to send senior officials here any time soon.
Lukashenko's chief aide, Ural Latypov, later dismissed Western criticism and predicted that the West would have to build a relationship with Belarus -- and Lukashenko.
"The West has got itself into a sticky situation," he said. "It's one thing to criticise a referendum before it's happened, but another once it has received wide support from the people".
"We are very interested in (U.S. Defence Secretary) William Perry and Russia's defence minister coming to the ceremony," he added.
But Lukashenko, in remarks interpreted by one analyst as a threat, made clear he did not care about Western criticism.
"I'm not scared of pressure. If they pressurise me, that will be their problem. It's a bit late to put pressure on me," he said. "And what's more, to crush me, that's impossible."
